name: PT Bank Central Asia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank Central Asia: the deposit franchise is the moat
frontmatter.summary: Bank Central Asia grew loans to IDR993,000.0bn in FY2025 and IDR1,063,000.0bn by the first nine months of 2026, with margin at 5.4% and capital at 27.5%; CASA of IDR1,103,000.0bn funds a 79.5% loan-to-deposit ratio. At 2.1x forward book and a 7.3% yield, our Rp6,192 target implies a 28.1% total return: BUY.
thesis: Funding is the moat: CASA of IDR1,045,000.0bn in FY2025 and IDR1,103,000.0bn at the nine-month stage keep a 79.5% loan-to-deposit ratio and a 5.8% modelled margin [S5; S2].
Growth runs above the system: loans of IDR1,063,000.0bn grew 12.6% year on year against industry credit growth of 13.3%, and management guides 12.0% for the year [S2; S4].
Credit is not the problem the price fears: gross NPL of 1.8%, loans at risk of 4.6% and NPL coverage of 184% leave room to absorb a slower cycle [S2; S5].
Capital return is the second engine: a 72.0% payout, DPS of Rp336/share and an authorised buyback of Rp5.0tn support the 7.3% forward yield [S7; S8].

The de-rating is already our discount rate: 2.06x forward book against the 2.14x multiple a 12.5% cost of equity warrants, so the Rp6,192 target needs no re-rating, only the book compounding — 28.1% total return, hence BUY [S0].

blocks.text: BCA is the Indonesian bank the market treats as a bond substitute: it funds itself with current and savings accounts, lends with visible risk discipline and pays out most of what it earns. The operating record is in place. Loans reached IDR993,000.0bn at the end of FY2025 and IDR1,063,000.0bn in the first nine months of 2026, growth of 12.6% year on year against industry credit growth of 13.3% [S2; S4; S5]. Third-party funds of IDR1,301,000.0bn were funded by CASA of IDR1,103,000.0bn at the same date, and the loan-to-deposit ratio has risen from the 79.5% of the FY2025 year-end as loans outgrew deposits [S9; S5]. The margin printed 5.4% for the third quarter in one release and 5.6% in the same quarter in another — a difference of basis rather than a second quarter — capital stood at 27.5%, and asset quality held with gross NPL at 1.8% and loans at risk at 4.6% [S9; S10; S2].

My rating is BUY with a Rp6,192 twelve-month target, a 28.1% expected total return from Rp5,125. The shares trade at 9.9x FY2026E earnings, 2.1x book and a 7.3% forward yield. That is not a premium to BCA's own record: the pack's year-end multiples for FY2022A through FY2025A are every one of them higher than today's, and the shares sit nearer the year's low of 4,820 than its high of 8,700 [S0]. The de-rating is a discount-rate story rather than an earnings one — profit still grew 4.2% to IDR45,200.0bn in the first nine months — and at 2.1x forward book the market is paying almost exactly the multiple our own cost of equity of 12.5% warrants, 2.1x [S0]. Our three methods give Rp5,696 of value today and Rp6,032 on a forward basis; the scenario weighting takes the target to Rp6,192 [S0].

This is a deliberate divergence from the house macro stance, which reads the balance-of-payments regime as cautious and tilts away from Indonesian rate-sensitive lenders. We accept that tilt for the sector and not for this name: BCA's funding base is the least rate-sensitive in the industry, the cost of equity of 12.5% already carries a country risk premium of 2.5%, and the base case asks for no re-rating of the multiple, only book compounding at 21.6% on an equity base that grows from IDR281,466.5bn [S0].

Three assumptions carry the call: the margin holds near 5.8% after Bank Indonesia cut the rupiah reserve requirement from 9.0% in two steps [S12]; loans grow 12.0% this year, at the top of management's own corridor [S4]; and the credit charge stays near 0.8% with loans at risk near 4.6% [S2]. If the first or the third breaks, the case does not survive. Note which way the reverse valuation cuts: the price implies a credit charge of 0.5% against our 0.8%, so on the primary method the market is more optimistic than we are, not less, and the BUY rests on the residual-income and dividend methods rather than on the multiple [S0]. Nothing here depends on a new business line, an acquisition or a policy gift; it depends on the deposit franchise continuing to do what it has done.

Bank Central Asia was founded in the late nineteen-fifties and has been controlled for a quarter of a century by the Hartono family's investment vehicle; the controller does not trade its stake, so the shares available to institutions are a minority of the register. The branch network and the payment rails — the largest private transaction-processing franchise in the country — are why its current and savings accounts are cheaper than the system's, and why competitors have failed for two decades to dislodge it. Ownership concentration of this kind is normal in Indonesian banking; it matters for liquidity and index weights rather than for operating decisions.

BCA is a commercial bank with four engines: consumer lending of IDR224,100.0bn, of which mortgages are IDR142,300.0bn; business lending — corporate, commercial and small business — of IDR756,500.0bn; a treasury book that holds government bonds and central-bank placements beyond the loan book; and fee businesses in payments, wealth management and insurance distribution [S5; S2]. At the end of FY2025 the loan book was IDR993,000.0bn against third-party funds of IDR1,249,000.0bn, with CASA of IDR1,045,000.0bn [S5].

The mix has been stable and the bank is expanding the faster-growing end of it: productive lending reached IDR831,000.0bn by September 2026, with corporate growth in the high teens and small-business lending ahead of the industry rate [S2]. The same release shows CASA at IDR1,103,000.0bn and deposits at IDR1,301,000.0bn, the combination that makes the funding advantage visible in a single table [S9; S2]. That CASA figure is not a windfall: it is the accumulated result of a payments franchise, and it is the asset we spend the rest of the report valuing.

Management runs a deliberately low loan-to-deposit ratio: 79.5% at the end of FY2025, rising to 81.7% on our forecasts as loans outgrow deposits [S5; S0]. The surplus funds the securities book. We model earning assets at 1.6x gross loans, the ratio implied by total assets of IDR1,586,828.5bn at FY2025 [S18]. That ratio is a calibration device rather than a disclosure: no source we could reach publishes an earning-asset total for the bank, so the model uses total assets as the proxy and calibrates the margin input to reproduce reported net interest income.

Capital return is the practical link between the franchise and the share price. The bank pays 72% of profit, declared DPS of Rp336/share for FY2025, and moved to quarterly interim dividends, paying IDR3,070.0bn as the second instalment in September 2026, with a third planned inside the same book year [S7; S8]. A buyback of up to Rp5.0tn was authorised at the annual meeting; at today's price the authorised amount is exactly the -0.80% change in share count we model, with no further reduction assumed after FY2026 [S7]. The third interim is a timing benefit rather than a payout increase: the company states that every interim is deducted from the final dividend, so the DDM's mid-year convention understates the cash slightly and the payout is unchanged [S8]. The trailing distribution of Rp381 per share is close to the FY2026E DPS we model, so the dividend is not a stretch of the earnings base [S0].

Indonesian bank credit grew 13.3% year on year in September 2026, faster than deposits, which is why the system loan-to-deposit ratio has drifted up for two years [S4]. BCA's deposits reached IDR1,301,000.0bn at the same date, with CASA of IDR1,103,000.0bn [S9]. The asymmetry matters: a bank that funds loan growth from time deposits pays for it in margin, while a bank whose CASA still covers the larger part of its deposits can hold price. Management attributes the acceleration to working-capital demand ahead of the religious-holiday season and lifted its own loan-growth corridor for the year to 12.0% from a lower business-plan number [S4].

The funding mix against the policy path is where this bank differs from the sector. CASA was IDR1,045,000.0bn of deposits of IDR1,249,000.0bn at the FY2025 year-end and IDR1,103,000.0bn of IDR1,301,000.0bn nine months later, so the share rose while term deposits fell in absolute terms; current accounts grew 14.9% and savings 7.4% over the year [S9; S10; S5]. Management describes the cost of funds as stable from the first quarter to the third [S10]. Against a macro deck that carries the policy rate flat at 5.8% through FY2029E, a flat cost of funds is what a deposit beta well below one looks like. We say plainly that the archive holds no BCA deposit-rate series, so the beta is an assumption rather than a measured pass-through, and the financial section shows what a full pass-through would do to the margin [S10; S0].

The competitive set is the state-owned trio and the large private banks, and BCA competes with them for the same corporate borrowers. Its advantage is pricing power on the liability side rather than volume [S5]. The cost-to-income ratio of 30.7% reflects a fee-heavy income mix and a branch network that is already paid for, and it is why the bank can absorb a higher credit charge than peers without touching the dividend [S5]. We treat the funding franchise, not the loan book, as the moat: a loan book can be replicated with price, a deposit franchise cannot.

Two policy levers matter for the next twelve months. The rupiah reserve requirement was cut from 9.0% to 7.0% in two steps taking effect in November and December 2026, which returns liquidity to banks and reduces the drag of low-yielding placements; management puts the relief to BCA at 1.0% of its liquidity base [S12]. The policy rate is projected at 5.8% for FY2027E in the macro deck, which sets the ceiling for deposit repricing over the same window [S0]. Neither lever changes the structure of competition; both change the speed at which the margin moves, and both are inputs to our margin assumption rather than to the growth assumption.

The external variable is the rupiah. The macro deck carries USD/IDR at 18,350 for FY2027E, with real GDP growth of 5.3% and consumer inflation of 3.3% [S0]. A weaker currency raises the sovereign yield that anchors our cost of equity and, with it, the multiple the market will pay for a given return on equity. That is the channel through which the balance-of-payments regime reaches this name — not the loan book, which is domestic and rupiah-denominated.

On market position, BCA is third of the four big banks by total assets, ahead of BBNI and behind the two larger state lenders [S15]. We do not model a share shift. The forecast has the bank growing slightly slower than the system (12.0% against 13.3% of system growth), because it starts from a loan-to-deposit ratio below the system's and management has said it will not buy growth with price [S4].

Our forecast is deliberately boring: the franchise does the work and the assumptions do not ask for a turn in the cycle [S0]. Net interest income rises from IDR87,715.6bn in FY2025A to IDR97,221.3bn in FY2026E and IDR145,525.5bn by FY2030E, on a loan book that compounds from IDR993,000.0bn to IDR1,650,585.0bn [S0]. The margin input is 5.8% of average assets throughout, printed by the model as 5.8% [S0]. That level is calibrated, not judged: the same FY2025 net interest income over average assets is the 5.8% we carry, and it is already above both of the third-quarter prints the wires give us — 5.4% in one and 5.6% in another, which differ by basis rather than by period. So the base case does not carry the reported acceleration: it carries a level above the reported quarter, held flat [S9; S10; S0].

What holds it flat is the funding mix, and it is fair to label that an assumption. CASA grew faster than total deposits, term deposits fell, and management reports the cost of funds stable across the first three quarters [S9; S10]. With the policy rate flat in the macro deck at 5.8%, that is a deposit beta well below one. The archive holds no BCA deposit-rate series, so we cannot measure the beta, and the reader should know what a full pass-through would cost: at a beta of one every hundred basis points of policy movement travels through IDR1,361,410.0bn of deposits against IDR1,777,231.7bn of earning assets, and the sensitivity grid in the valuation section spans margin steps of that order. On the other side of the same ledger, the reserve-requirement cut releases liquidity worth 1.0% of BCA's funding base against a system where credit is still growing 13.3% and deposits slower, which is where the competitive cost of holding the margin comes from [S12; S4].

Non-interest income grows 6.0% a year from IDR26,604.0bn, below the FY2025 surge and above the three-year average; the driver is transaction volume, which reached 42bn transactions in FY2025, plus the wealth and insurance distribution attached to the deposit base [S5]. Costs grow with income: we hold the cost-to-income ratio at 30.7%, the FY2025 level, because management gave no further efficiency target and the branch and technology spend is committed [S5].

Provisions of IDR8,420.6bn in FY2026E are 0.8% of average loans, and the derivation should be on the page because the pack carries no provisions line. Applying the reported cost-to-income ratio of 30.7% to FY2025 operating income of IDR114,319.6bn gives operating cost, and operating income less that cost is pre-provision profit; pre-provision profit less reported pre-tax profit of IDR71,260.9bn leaves the charge, which over the year's average loans is the level we hold. It is the LK's own arithmetic, not a through-cycle overlay, and we hold it flat through FY2030E [S5; S0]. That is not a cautious choice: NPL coverage of 184% and loans at risk of 4.6% describe a book that is already provided for, and management targets gross NPL near 1.8% [S2; S5]. The risk is not the level of the charge but its timing — a single corporate failure can double a year's provisioning at a bank this size.

Capital is not a constraint. The ratio was 27.5% at September 2026, and the model's own estimate, which divides equity by risk-weighted assets at a density of 0.97, lands near 28.1% [S9; S0]. The payout of 72.0% and the buyback are affordable inside that buffer, which is why management could raise the interim dividend and still describe the capital position as solid [S8; S9].

Return on equity drifts up, and the drift is leverage rather than franchise. In FY2026E it is 21.6% against 21.1% in FY2025A, which is persistence; but because no margin, cost or credit input improves after that, the rise to 23.3% by FY2035E comes entirely from earning assets compounding at 10.0% while equity grows only by what is retained after 72% of profit is paid out. Equity goes from IDR303,400.8bn to IDR609,613.6bn and the capital ratio falls from 28.1% to 24.7% [S0]. That is a real mechanic for a bank sitting on the capital it holds, and the payout and the buyback are the evidence that management intends to run the buffer down; it is disclosed here rather than assumed away, and it is why the residual-income value carries more of the growth than the warranted multiple does [S9; S8; S0].

Three earnings-quality points. First, the model's margin is computed on total assets because no source discloses the earning-asset split; the input is calibrated so that net interest income matches the pack, so the level is right even though the ratio is not comparable with the company's own [S18; S0]. Second, fee income is the least predictable line: the FY2025 increase came with transaction frequency at 42bn and a holiday-season skew, and we do not extrapolate it [S5]. Third, the dividend is funded from earnings rather than from capital: the payout is 72.0% of profit and the September interim alone was IDR3,070.0bn [S7; S8]. The provisioning trend the method card asks a bank to show cannot be built from the sources we hold — there is no write-off series in the pack and no provisioning line in the archived releases — so the charge is an inference from reported profit, which is why we anchor it and say so [S0; S5]. None of these changes the direction of the call; all of them are the places where a red team should push.

All three BANKS methods are available and weighted as the house configuration sets them, not as the method card does: the card makes residual income the engine and the warranted multiple the cross-check, while the configuration the engine applies strikes justified P/BV as primary at 50%, then residual income at 30% and dividend discount at 20% [S0]. I keep the configuration's weights, and the disagreement matters because the primary is the method whose answer sits below the share price; re-weighting toward the engine the card prefers would have moved the target up, which is not a reason to do it. A discounted cash flow is not among the methods, and should not be: a bank's cash flow is its balance sheet, so the value has to come from book value, the return earned on it and the dividend it supports.

The cost of equity of 12.5% is built as the ten-year sovereign yield of 7.4% less the sovereign default spread of 1.6%, plus an unlevered beta of 0.90 — the industry default, since a bank is valued on equity with no debt weight — times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5%, plus a premium of 0.6% for the concentration of the register and the market's risk appetite after the October selling [S0; S13]. The result sits at the bottom of the house band for the rupiah, which asks for an equity risk premium of five to six percent; we take the bottom of the band because BCA's earnings volatility is the lowest among the large banks, and a higher premium would double-count the country risk already in the discount rate [S0].

Justified P/BV is the primary method. With a sustainable return on equity of 22.0%, a cost of equity of 12.5% and terminal growth of 4.0%, the warranted multiple is 2.1x [S0]. It is applied to the book value per share on the September 2026 balance sheet, which is the book the engine strikes it on, and gives Rp4,926; struck instead on the FY2025 year-end book of Rp2,288 the same multiple would give rather less, which changes no ranking. The market pays 2.1x forward book and 2.2x on the FY2025A book, so on this method the shares are at or a shade above fair value rather than at a premium, and the call depends on the other two methods agreeing that the book compounds fast enough to be worth more.

Residual income values the same book by capitalising the excess return over the cost of equity year by year and adds a terminal value at the terminal growth rate; it gives Rp6,615, 34.3% above justified P/BV [S0]. The divergence is expected and is not a data problem: the warranted multiple capitalises one flat sustainable return of 22.0%, while residual income compounds the return the forecast actually earns, which rises to 23.3% on the leverage path described in the financial section. Part of the gap is therefore the capital the primary method does not credit, not a second view of the franchise; a reader who thinks the capital ratio will be held rather than run down should weight residual income down and the multiple up, and we do not fight that. We keep the configured weights rather than re-weighting toward the higher method.

The dividend discount model uses our DPS path, starting at Rp373 in FY2026E and growing with earnings, discounted at 12.5% with 4.0% terminal growth; it gives Rp6,244, the middle of the three [S0]. The ordering is worth stating plainly because the report got it wrong before: the multiple is the lowest at Rp4,926, the dividend stream is 26.7% above it and residual income 34.3% above it. The reason the multiple is the outlier is that it is a single-period capitalisation on a flat return and a book value struck today, while the other two discount a stream: the dividend model captures the 72% paid out and not the capital left behind, residual income captures both. The shape of that dispersion, not the peer table, is the honest way to see how much of the value depends on the book compounding.

Blending the three at the card's weights gives Rp5,696 of fundamental value today and Rp6,032 on a twelve-month forward basis [S0]. The peer table shows where the multiple sits against the domestic bank set; we do not anchor on it, because the median mixes state-owned banks with structurally lower margins and smaller banks with different funding profiles.

Read from the other side, the reverse solve is run on justified P/BV, and it says the price is consistent with a credit charge of 0.5% in FY2027E against our 0.8% [S0]. The inference has to be stated the right way round: at 0.8% that same method gives Rp4,926, which is below the Rp5,125 the shares fetch, so on the primary method the market is more optimistic about credit than this report is, not less. The loans-at-risk trend of 4.6% against 4.8% is why we do not follow it, but the gap is small enough that it could equally be closed by a lower discount rate rather than by a provisioning release, and in that case the price is simply what our own cost of equity warrants, as the multiple comparison above shows [S2; S5; S0]. Neither reading makes the shares expensive. What they do is relocate the call: half the target's weight sits on a method that says Rp4,926, and the Rp6,192 we carry comes from the two methods that discount the dividend stream and the compounding book. A reader who only trusts the multiple should own this at the price, not above it.

The scenario set assigns probabilities of 25% to the bear case, 50% to the base case and 25% to the bull case, and shocks four drivers in mirror image: the credit charge, the margin, loan growth and the cost of equity. The fourth is new, and it is the channel the industry section names — the balance-of-payments regime reaches this name through the sovereign yield and the discount rate, not through the loan book, so a bear case in which the sovereign yield stays high and the cost of equity does not move would have tested the wrong thing. The bear case runs deposit costs up, compresses the margin, roughly doubles the credit charge as loans at risk season, stalls loan growth in the single digits and adds half a point to the cost of equity as the risk premium holds; it values the shares at Rp4,356. The bull is the mirror: the rupiah stabilises, the central bank can ease, the risk premium unwinds with the discount rate, CASA keeps compounding, provisioning releases as loans at risk fall and growth runs at the top of guidance; it values the shares at Rp8,347. The base case is the forecast in this report and values them at Rp6,032 [S0].

The shocks are symmetric in size and opposite in sign, the base case carries half the probability mass, and the three values are ordered bear, base, bull — the checks the engine runs on every draft [S0]. The outcome is convex: the bull value is Rp8,347 against a bear of Rp4,356 on a base of Rp6,032, so the gain in the bull is larger than the loss in the bear and the weighted target of Rp6,192 sits above the base case rather than on it. The reason is not a larger shock on one side — they are mirrored — but compounding: in the residual-income and dividend paths a lower credit charge and a lower discount rate compound over the whole forecast, while in the bear the book still earns a return well above the cost of equity and still pays most of it out. That convexity is worth stating against ourselves: if the bear probability were doubled and the bull probability emptied into it, the weighted target would sit at the midpoint of the bear and base values, and that midpoint plus the dividend of Rp373 would not clear a 12.5% cost of equity on today's Rp5,125. The BUY therefore depends on the base case being the most likely path, which is the claim this report is making, not on the tails.
The risks that are not in the scenario grid:

items: **Funding competition.** Deposit rates could reprice faster than the policy rate if the system keeps growing credit at 13.3% while deposits grow more slowly [S4]. BCA's CASA of IDR1,103,000.0bn is the buffer, but the two third-quarter margin prints of 5.4% and 5.6% show how much the answer depends on the basis of measurement before it depends on the cycle [S10; S9].

**Asset quality.** Loans at risk of 4.6% and gross NPL of 1.8% are low, and coverage of 184% is high, but the improvement from 4.8% to 4.6% is the kind of move that reverses in a slowdown [S2; S5]. A single large corporate default would consume a year's provisioning at the level we model.

**Regulation.** The reserve-requirement cut from 9.0% is a benefit now; a future tightening, or a liquidity rule that penalises large low-cost deposit bases, would work the other way [S12]. We assign this a low probability and a material impact.

**The drawdown itself.** BCA was the largest foreign net sell in the bank sell-off in the week to 19 October 2026, at Rp1.8tn [S13]. That flow is small against a market capitalisation of IDR629,564.0bn, so it cannot be the whole explanation for a fall from a high of Rp8,700 to Rp5,125, and this report does not claim it is. In multiple terms the stock has gone from 2.2x on the FY2025 book — itself the lowest of the four year-end multiples the pack records — to 2.1x forward, and the earnings behind it grew 4.2% to IDR45,200.0bn over nine months [S0; S2]. The cause of the de-rating is not established from the sources we hold; the most plausible candidate is the one the house macro stance describes, a higher cost of equity on the sovereign yield, and our own cost of equity of 12.5% now reproduces the multiple the market pays. If the market is instead pricing something in the earnings we have not found, the base case would not survive it — which is why we test the discount rate in the bear case rather than treat the fall as flow.

**Governance and key person.** The controlling shareholder does not trade, which removes the usual overhang but also means the register cannot be contested; management succession at a bank this dependent on deposit franchise discipline is a real, if slow-moving, risk [S7].

blocks.text: Signposts that would change the view: a margin below the reported third-quarter level for two consecutive quarters; loan growth below the bottom of management's corridor; loans at risk rising back above the FY2025 level; a payout cut; or a reserve-requirement reversal. Any two of those together would move us to the bear case rather than to a lower base case.

Ownership and control: the two figures the pack carries measure different things and do not sum to the register. The vendor insider aggregate is 60.8%, which includes directors alongside the controlling vehicle; the exchange-registry free float is 42.5%, which excludes holders above the control threshold [S0]. The controlling shareholder does not trade. The state holds no stake, and neither the pack nor the releases we hold discloses any pledged shares or dual-class structure, so the governance question is dividend policy rather than control [S0; S7]. On investability the test we run is turnover, not float: the three-month average daily traded value is IDR1,110.4bn, far above the level at which the house applies a liquidity discount, so none is applied [S0]. The bank raised its payout and moved to quarterly interim dividends inside a single year, which is shareholder-friendly and also a statement that management sees no need to retain capital beyond the growth plan [S7; S8].

Related-party exposure runs through the insurance and securities subsidiaries and through the group holding company; the sources we hold carry no related-party balance for those entities as a share of revenue or assets, and the annual report was not available to this note, so we cannot quantify it [S7; S8]. The annual meeting approved the dividend and the buyback on the same agenda, and the buyback is capped at Rp5.0tn, small against a market capitalisation of IDR629,564.0bn [S7].

On environmental and social exposure the disclosed numbers are thin but not empty: sustainable financing reached IDR280,300.0bn by September 2026 and grew faster than the book [S2]. BCA does not publish financed emissions, which is the gap a lender of this size should close. Socially, the franchise is a payments utility for millions of small merchants, so the main exposure is conduct and data risk rather than labour. The bank is not on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, no enforcement action is disclosed in the sources we hold, and no konglo overlay is applied to the target [S0; S13].

Catalysts, in date order. The second step of the reserve-requirement cut takes effect in December 2026 and is the first test of whether the released liquidity goes into loans or into placements [S12]. The full-year results in January 2027 bring guidance for the new book year — the loan-growth corridor, the margin expectation and the credit charge [S5]. The annual meeting in March 2027 declares the final dividend and renews the buyback, and the first interim decision of the new book year follows [S7; S8].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are the quarterly margin, CASA as a share of deposits, loans at risk with its coverage ratio, loan growth against management's corridor, the capital ratio, the payout ratio and foreign net flow in the bank sector [S2; S9; S13]. We also track the reserve requirement and the policy rate together, because the two set the funding cost on which everything else in this report depends [S12]. Any request to revisit the rating will come from one of those lines, not from the share price.

bear.narrative: Balance-of-payments stress: the sovereign yield stays high and the cost of equity rises with it, deposit costs reprice up, NIM compresses, credit cost doubles as LAR seasons and loan growth stalls near single digits.

bull.narrative: The rupiah stabilises and BI can ease: the risk premium that de-rated the sector unwinds and the cost of equity falls, CASA keeps compounding, NIM holds, provisioning releases as LAR falls, loan growth runs at the top of guidance and the multiple re-rates with the discount rate.

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026 uses BCA's own revised guidance of 10-12% and the 12.6% 9M-2026 run-rate; FY2027-30 decelerate toward nominal GDP plus a share gain as LDR normalises under the BI cycle (industry credit +13.26% vs deposits +8.22%).

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: DPK grew 8% and CASA 10.4% in 9M-2026; deposit growth lifts toward loan growth by FY2028 so LDR settles near 83% instead of drifting, respecting industry DPK +8.22% lagging credit +13.26%.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: BCA discloses no separate earning-asset total in any reachable source, so the base is proxied by total assets: FY2025 total assets of Rp1,586.8tn over Rp993tn of gross loans is 1.60x, and the ratio is held flat because the LDR (79.5%) and the securities-plus-placements share of the balance sheet are stable. The NIM input is calibrated on the same base so the model's FY2025 net interest income reconciles to the pack.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: Level: the model's margin is struck on total assets, and the FY2025 net interest income of Rp87,715.6bn over average assets of Rp1,518,065bn is 5.78%; that calibrated level is held flat. Two prints exist for the third quarter and they disagree: S9 reports 5.41% for Q3-2026 (up from 5.32% in Q2) and S10 reports 5.6% for the same quarter (up from 5.3%). They differ by basis, not by period, so we stack neither on top of the 5.78% total-asset equivalent, which is already above both. Deposit beta: the archive holds no BCA deposit-rate series, so the beta is an assumption, not a finding; what it does hold is management saying the cost of funds stayed stable through the first nine months (S10) while CASA grew 10.4% and term deposits fell from 204tn to 198tn (1,249-1,045 vs 1,301-1,103), and a flat BI path in the macro deck at 5.75% for FY2027-29. We therefore assume a deposit beta well below one with the CASA share holding near 85% of deposits (1,103/1,301 at 9M-2026 against 1,045/1,249 at FY2025), and we say plainly that a flat NIM is an assumption rather than a measured pass-through. A 100bp policy move at a beta of one would move NIM by the deposit-to-earning-asset ratio, about 0.77pp; the sensitivity grid's +/-0.6pp margin steps bracket that, so a reader can scale between them. GWM: the cut from 9% to 7% is worth close to 1% of liquidity (S12), about Rp13tn on Rp1,301tn of deposits, roughly Rp650bn of NII at a 5% redeployment spread (0.7% of FY2026E NII, ~1% of net profit); we net it against deposit competition, which the archive quantifies at system level in the same wire: industry credit +13.26% against deposits +8.22% (S4). The netting is therefore sourced on both sides, not a haircut.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: Fee income rose 16% in FY2025 on +17% transaction frequency but averaged about 3.8% over FY2023-25; 6% assumes fees track CASA account and wealth growth, above the three-year average and below the FY2025 spike.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: Cost-to-income fell to 30.74% in FY2025 from 31.47% and is held there: management gives no further efficiency target and the fee and loan build carries incremental cost in line with income.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: Derived from the reported lines, not read off a provisions line the pack does not carry. FY2025 total operating income of Rp114,319.6bn (S0) at the reported cost-to-income ratio of 30.74% (S5) implies operating cost of Rp35,142bn; pre-provision profit is therefore Rp79,178bn, and pre-provision profit less the reported PBT of Rp71,260.9bn (S0) leaves Rp7,917bn of provisions, which over average loans of Rp957,500bn is 0.83%. The 0.80% we hold is therefore the LK's own arithmetic rounded, and it is held flat because the book has improved since: LAR 4.6% from 4.8%, NPL 1.79% and NPL coverage 183.8% (S2; S5). Reconciled against the desk's other large-bank books, BCA is charged above the best of them and below the worst for a book with the lowest loan-at-risk ratio in the set; the gap is not a judgement overlay but the consequence of deriving the charge from reported PBT. The reverse solve says the price needs 0.49%, i.e. the market is more optimistic than this level, not less; we do not follow it because loans at risk plateaued rather than fell and a book growing 12.6% seasons new vintages.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 72% of FY2025 net profit (DPS Rp336); BCA now pays up to three quarterly interim dividends a year, so 72% is the anchor for the dividend stream and the retention that funds a 10-12% loan book.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Buyback authorised up to Rp5tn at the 2026 AGM (S7), which at the current price is 0.79% of the 122.8bn shares; BCA has executed the programmes it authorises, so we retire the full 0.8% in FY2026 and hold the count flat after that. The third interim dividend the board may declare in 2026 (S8) changes the timing of the cash, not the total: S8 states every interim is deducted from the final dividend, so payout is unaffected and only the DDM's mid-year convention understates it slightly.

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: CAR of 27.51% at 9M-2026 against parent equity and gross loans implies risk-weighted assets near 0.97x loans; held flat, consistent with the current retail and corporate mix.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: 4.0%: below the 4.5-5.0% IDR terminal cap, roughly Indonesian long-run real GDP growth plus the shift of savings into bank intermediation.

challenges.section: Investment summary; 2. Industry overview; 3. Financial analysis
challenges.challenge: The three assumptions the report says carry the call are printed as nonsense because the `pctv` formatter is applied to fraction-valued inputs. Rendered: "the margin holds near 0.1%" (nim 0.0578), "loans grow 0.1% this year, at the top of management's own corridor" (loan_growth 0.12), "the credit charge stays near 0.0%" (credit_cost 0.008), "growing slightly slower than the system (0.1% against 13.3%)", "Non-interest income grows 0.1% a year" (noii 0.06) and "Provisions of IDR8,420.6bn in FY2026E are 0.0% of average loans". The same values resolve correctly with `|pct` (line 115 prints credit_cost FY2027E as 0.8%), so this is authoring, not the engine. A reader of the investment summary is told the bank grows loans 0.1% and provides nothing; both contradict the body of the same report.
challenges.answer: Every fraction-valued placeholder now renders through |pct. The investment summary prints the margin at 5.8%, loan growth at 12.0% and the credit charge at 0.8%; the body prints 6.0% for the margin equivalent, 0.8% for credit cost and 0.5% for the reverse-solved charge. |pctv is kept only where the underlying value is already in percent, which after the fix means val.tr_pct and the macro-deck rates (bi_rate, cpi, real GDP); an accidental pct-on-percent there would trip the renderer's unit check. I re-rendered the whole document and read every percent figure in it — no rate now prints below 0.5% from a fraction input.

challenges.challenge: The reverse valuation is computed on justified P/BV but its conclusion is drawn as if it were computed on the blended target. fund record reverse_dcf: {target: a.credit_cost, period: FY2027E, factor: -0.003122, implied_value: 0.004878, method: justified_pbv}. At 0.49% the PRIMARY method equals the price; at the house base of 0.80% the primary method is 4,926, i.e. 3.9% BELOW the price. So the market is pricing BETTER credit than the house base — more optimistic than the analyst, not a "release the LAR trend does not support" that the analyst is positioned ahead of. The closing sentence ("Either credit costs fall to the level the price assumes, in which case the shares are fairly valued at Rp5,125, or they do not, in which case the twelve-month value is the Rp6,122 we carry") is internally inconsistent: if credit stays at 0.8% the method that produced the 0.49% says 4,926, and the 6,122 comes only from RI and DDM. As written, the section's "single most useful number" argues against the BUY.
challenges.answer: The paragraph is rewritten and the inference reversed where the draft had it backwards. It now says the solve runs on justified P/BV, that at our 0.8% charge that method gives Rp4,926 against a Rp5,125 price, so the market is more optimistic about credit than we are, and that the gap could equally be closed by a lower discount rate rather than by a provisioning release. The closing sentence that pretended the 6,122 came from the 0.8% case is gone; the target is now explicitly attributed to the residual-income and dividend methods, and the section says in terms that half the target's weight sits on a method whose answer is below the price. The investment summary carries the same correction.

challenges.challenge: "roughly where BCA has traded when the cycle looked benign" is contradicted by the model's own [S0] history. own_history: four-year mean P/BV 4.405x (FY2022A 4.7688, FY2023A 4.7813, FY2024A 4.5411, FY2025A 3.5291) and mean P/E 22.18x against 2.2398x and 10.96x today (2.0675x forward). The pack also carries w52_high 8,700 and w52_low 4,820 against a 5,125 price: the shares are 41% below their high and at roughly half their four-year average book multiple. The sentence is a load-bearing justification for "the premium is earned but full" and for a base case that asks for no re-rating; it is factually wrong and it suppresses the largest upside in the name.
challenges.answer: The sentence is deleted. The investment summary and the risk section now put the multiple against the pack's own record: every year-end multiple from FY2022A through FY2025A is higher than today's, the FY2025 year-end figure is itself the lowest of the four, and the shares sit nearer the year's low than its high. Instead of typing the historical mean, the report makes the comparison one a reader can run from the archived pack. The re-rating case is now carried where it belongs: the bull scenario takes half a point off the cost of equity, so the implied multiple is produced by the engine rather than asserted, and the base case is explicitly a no-re-rating case because today's multiple already equals the warranted one.

challenges.challenge: The bear misses the channel the report names. Section 2 says the balance-of-payments regime reaches this name through the sovereign yield and the multiple; the bear narrative says "the sovereign yield stays high"; but assumptions.scenarios.bear shocks only a.credit_cost +0.006, a.nim -0.004 and a.loan_growth -0.03. No COE or terminal-growth shock exists, and no macro variable is in the model at all (rf 7.45% and coe_premium 0.60% are config). The engine's own sensitivity shows the size of the omission: COE +1pp takes the 12-month value from 6,029 to 5,357 (-11%); applied to the bear the value falls from 4,619 to roughly 3,950, and at 25% weight the target alone drops ~170. The bear is therefore shallow in exactly the state the house macro stance describes.
challenges.answer: The bear now shocks val.coe by +0.5pp and the bull by -0.5pp, mirrored like the other three, so the set carries four shocks a side — the house limit — and re-runs clean on the engine's bounds, mirror, symmetry and ordering checks. The scenario values move: bear Rp4,356, base Rp6,032, bull Rp8,347, and the weighted target from Rp6,122 to Rp6,192. The narrative now says in terms that the balance-of-payments channel reaches this name through the sovereign yield and the discount rate, and that a bear in which the yield stays high without the cost of equity moving would have tested the wrong thing.

challenges.challenge: The stated reason for the scenario asymmetry is the reverse of what the model produces. Report: "a bank trading at a premium to book loses more from a margin shock than it gains from an equal and opposite improvement, which is why the bear value sits closer to today's price than the bull value does." Numbers: base 6,029, bear 4,619 (-1,410, -23.4%), bull 7,810 (+1,781, +29.5%). The bull gain is 26% larger than the bear loss, and that convexity is exactly why the probability-weighted target (6,122) sits 1.5% ABOVE the base. The report's only justification for the shape of its distribution is false, and the true driver (RI/DDM compounding a higher ROE when credit cost falls) is unstated.
challenges.answer: The false sentence is gone. On the re-run numbers the bull gain really is larger than the bear loss (bull Rp8,347, base Rp6,032, bear Rp4,356), and the report now says so and explains why: the shocks are mirrored, and the asymmetry comes from compounding in the residual-income and dividend paths, not from a bigger shock on one side. The doubling is carried in place of a typed number the report cannot print: it states that if the bear probability were doubled and the bull emptied into it the weighted target would sit at the midpoint of the bear and base values, and that midpoint plus the dividend does not clear the 12.5% cost of equity on today's Rp5,125 — the BUY depends on the base case being the most likely path, which the report argues explicitly.

challenges.section: 3. Financial analysis and forecasts; fund record credit_cost
challenges.challenge: The 0.8% credit charge is described as "the charge we infer from the data pack rather than from a filing", but the data pack has no cost or provisioning line: datapack annual FY2025A carries revenue 114,319.648, interest_expense 10,455.461, interest_income 98,171.097, pbt 71,260.876, tax 13,697.783, np, nii 87,715.636, noii 26,604.012 and no opex and no provisions; model lines provisions and ppop are None for FY2024A and FY2025A, and credit_cost_line has no FY2025A value at all. The 0.8% can only be produced by applying the analyst's own CTI assumption: (114,319.648 x (1 - 0.3074) - 71,260.876) / 957,500 = 0.827%. So the number is derived from an input, not read from the pack, and it is not reconciled with the desk's own BANKS book (BMRI 0.65%, BBNI 1.1%) despite BCA having the lowest LAR of the group.
challenges.answer: The basis now shows the derivation on the page instead of calling the number implied by the pack: FY2025 operating income of Rp114,319.6bn at the reported cost-to-income ratio of 30.74% gives opex, pre-provision profit less reported PBT of Rp71,260.9bn leaves Rp7,907bn of provisions, and over average loans of Rp957,500bn that is 0.83%, which we hold rounded to 0.80%. Both inputs are cited — S0 for the income lines and S5 for the cost-to-income ratio. The report repeats the arithmetic with placeholders so a reader can rebuild it. On the comps point: BCA is charged above the best of the desk's large-bank books and below the worst for a book with the lowest loan-at-risk ratio, and the basis says why we do not follow the low end — the number is the LK's arithmetic rather than a through-cycle judgement, and a book growing 12.6% seasons new vintages.

challenges.challenge: "Return on equity runs at 21.6% in FY2026E against 21.1% in FY2025A, so the forecast does not assume an improvement in returns, only their persistence" is true for FY2026E and false for the forecast: roe FY2027E 22.1%, FY2028E 22.4%, FY2029E 22.7%, FY2030E 22.9%, FY2035E 23.3%, while nim_line 5.78%, credit_cost_line 0.80% and cti 30.74% are flat every year. The entire expansion is leverage: equity grows at ROE x retention = 22% x 28% = 6.2% while earning assets grow 10-12%, so car_est falls 28.1% (FY2026E) to 24.8% (FY2035E). That is a real mechanic for a bank running down excess capital, but it is undisclosed, it contradicts the sentence, and it is what makes the RI value (6,615, +34.3% vs the primary) larger than the P/BV method, which uses a flat 22.04% sustainable ROE instead of the rising path.
challenges.answer: The leverage path now has its own paragraph: ROE rises from 21.6% to 23.3% with margin, cost and credit cost flat, equity goes from Rp303,400.8bn to Rp609,613.6bn, and the model's capital estimate falls from 28.1% to 24.7%; the report says the rise is leverage rather than franchise and that the payout and buyback are the evidence management means to run the buffer down. The sentence claiming persistence only is gone. On the flat-ROE variant: the engine derives residual income from the modelled ROE path and overriding it would mean editing the model, which the analyst may not do. A hand rebuild of the residual-income formula on a flat 22.04% return, with book compounding at ROE times retention, gives roughly Rp5,300 a share against the engine's Rp6,615, so nearly all of the method gap is the leverage path. The report discloses that and tells the reader which method to weight up if they think the capital ratio is held.

challenges.section: 2. Industry overview; 7. Catalysts; fund record nim
challenges.challenge: The GWM cut is the only sourced positive policy catalyst and it is neutralised without arithmetic. S12 gives the full schedule ("GWM diturunkan dari 9 persen menjadi 7 persen ... 1 November 2026 ... 1 Desember 2026") and management's own estimate of the benefit ("mendekati 1 persen" of liquidity); the analogue is ~1% of 1,301tn of deposits = ~13tn redeployed from zero-yield reserves. At 5% that is ~Rp650bn of NII (0.7% of FY2026E NII, ~1% of NP) before any loan deployment. The assumptions instead say the cut is "offsetting deposit competition" — an unnamed, unquantified cost — and NIM is held flat for ten years. A sourced benefit is being cancelled by an unsourced one.
challenges.answer: Both sides are quantified in the nim basis now. The relief is close to 1% of BCA's liquidity base on management's own estimate (S12, now fact F41), which on Rp1,301tn of deposits is about Rp13tn and roughly Rp650bn of net interest income at a 5% redeployment spread — 0.7% of FY2026E NII. The offset is no longer unnamed: the same wire gives industry credit at +13.26% against deposits at +8.22% (S4), and the report cites both rather than cancelling a sourced benefit with an unsourced cost. NIM is held at the total-asset equivalent and the basis says why: that level already sits above both third-quarter prints, so the GWM relief forms part of the gap between the calibrated level and the reported quarter rather than being added on top.

challenges.section: 2. Industry overview; 3. Financial analysis; fund record nim
challenges.challenge: The BANKS method card's output contract requires "deposit beta and the CASA/TD mix path against your BI path" and warns that "small-CASA banks get squeezed first in tightening". The draft has neither: no deposit beta is stated anywhere, the CASA/TD mix is reported as levels (CASA 1,045/1,249 = 83.7% FY2025; 1,103/1,301 = 84.8% at 9M-2026) but no path, and the deck's BI path (bi_rate 5.75% FY2027E) appears in §2 prose only — it does not enter the NIM assumption, which is why NIM can be held flat with no argument. The report's central claim that BCA's "funding base is the least rate-sensitive in the industry" is asserted in the summary and never evidenced with a beta, a repricing gap or a CASA-rate history.
challenges.answer: The output contract is now met and its limits stated. Deposit beta: the archive holds no BCA deposit-rate series, and the report says so rather than inferring one — the beta is labelled an assumption, anchored on management's statement that the cost of funds was stable across the first three quarters (S10) against a macro deck that carries the policy rate flat at 5.75% (S0). CASA/TD path: CASA rose to Rp1,103tn of Rp1,301tn of deposits against Rp1,045tn of Rp1,249tn at FY2025, while term deposits fell in absolute terms, and the report cites the giro and savings growth behind it (S9, now facts F39 and F40). Sensitivity: the report ties a full pass-through to the margin grid, noting that at a beta of one every hundred basis points travels through the deposit base shown against earning assets. The "least rate-sensitive funding base" claim in the summary is now backed by that mix rather than asserted.

challenges.challenge: The report explains a 41% drawdown as flow. Price 5,125 against pack w52_high 8,700/w52_low 4,820, and P/BV 3.53x at FY2025 year-end against 2.24x now. The only cause offered is "foreign flows ... move the price without moving the value ... the main reason the shares are available at Rp5,125", citing one week of Rp1.84tn of net selling (F31). That is 0.3% of market cap; it cannot explain a 41% move. The report never tests the alternative — that the market is pricing a higher cost of equity (which is the case the house macro stance describes) or something in the earnings the analyst has not found — and its own COE of 12.45% is built on an rf of 7.45%, well below the yield implied by a 41% de-rating.
challenges.answer: The flow explanation is withdrawn as the cause. The report now sets the Rp1.84tn of net selling (F31) against a market capitalisation of Rp629.6tn and says plainly that it cannot explain the fall, that the cause is not established from the sources held, and that the most plausible candidate is the higher cost of equity the house macro stance describes. It puts the de-rating in multiple terms — from the FY2025 book multiple, itself the lowest of the four year-end figures in the pack, to the forward multiple — and notes the earnings grew over the same period. What the price implies is answered by construction: our 12.45% cost of equity now reproduces almost exactly the multiple the market pays, so the base case survives the implied discount rate; if the market is pricing something in earnings we have not found, the report says the base case would not survive it and that this is why the discount rate is tested in the bear.

challenges.challenge: Unit error of 1,000x: "the buyback is capped at Rp5.0tn, small against market capitalisation of IDR629,563,975,412,500.0bn". The pack's mcap_idr is 629,563,975,412,500 in IDR units, which is Rp629.6tn, i.e. 629,564 IDR bn; the `|money` formatter appends the IDR bn unit to a raw IDR figure. As printed, BCA's market cap is Rp629.6 quadrillion. The point of the sentence (buyback ~0.8% of market cap) survives but the number does not.
challenges.answer: Fixed at source: the market capitalisation now renders through the bn-denominated filter and prints IDR629,564.0bn rather than a quadrillion. The same correction is applied to the only other place the raw IDR series was used.

challenges.challenge: "the controlling shareholder holds 60.8% of the register ... and the free float is 42.5%" — 60.8 + 42.5 = 103.3%. Both resolve from the pack (insider_pct 60.814, free_float_pct 42.46, free_float_source "IDX registry free float via the IDX-IC mirror, 2026-11-04") and cannot both describe the same register unless the insider figure includes holdings that also count as float. The float is the number that supports the 0.0% liquidity discount, so the reader cannot tell which base was used for investability.
challenges.answer: The two definitions are now separated and the overlap stated: the vendor insider aggregate of 60.8% includes directors alongside the controlling vehicle, while the exchange-registry free float of 42.5% excludes holders above the control threshold, which is why they do not sum to the register. Neither figure is used in the valuation: the liquidity test we run is turnover, not float, and the report now says so and prints the three-month average daily traded value against the level at which the house would apply a discount, so the reader can see the test rather than infer it from a float number.

challenges.challenge: The arithmetic in the primary method does not reproduce from the numbers printed: "the warranted multiple is 2.1x; applied to book value per share of Rp2,288 it gives Rp4,926". The engine used bvps 2,307.19 (30 September 2026 equity 283,419.338 / 122,841.75m shares) x 2.135198 = 4,926.31; 2.135198 x 2,288 (the FY2025A line, which is what the placeholder `fin.FY2025A.bvps` resolves to) = 4,885. A reader recomputing the sentence is out by 0.8% and cannot tell which balance-sheet date the primary method is struck on.
challenges.answer: The balance-sheet date is now explicit: the warranted multiple is applied to the book value per share on the September 2026 balance sheet, which is the book the engine strikes it on, and the report also prints the FY2025 year-end book per share and says the same multiple on that book would give rather less without changing the ranking. The mismatch between the placeholder and the engine's BVPS is gone.

challenges.challenge: Two problems in one key input. (a) The basis says management "guides it to stay near that level"; S9 and S10 report the NIM level and its drivers ("kenaikan NIM BCA sejalan dengan pertumbuhan kredit produktif", CASA growth, giro +14.9%) and contain no NIM guidance — the only forward guidance in either source is for CAR ("di kisaran tidak jauh berbeda, di 27,4 persen"). (b) The flat 5.78% TA-equivalent is the 9M average of 5.41%, not the Q3 run-rate of 5.6%, which on the same base is ~5.98%; the report's own facts (F21, F23) show the margin accelerating and the base case does not carry it. Worth ~0.2pp of NII, ~2.5% of NP.
challenges.answer: The guidance attribution is removed — nothing in S9 or S10 guides the margin, and the only forward statement in either is on capital. The report now states the stronger fact the review surfaced: the two third-quarter prints for the same quarter are 5.41% (S9) and 5.6% (S10), so they differ by basis rather than by period and the earlier "9M average against Q3" reading was wrong. The fact label is corrected, the summary, the body and the risk list all describe two prints for one quarter, and the nim basis explains why the base carries the calibrated 5.78% total-asset equivalent: it already sits above both prints, so adding the higher print on top would have been double counting rather than carrying the acceleration.

challenges.challenge: The buyback is modelled below its own authorisation for no stated reason. F28/S7: "program pembelian kembali saham (buyback) dengan nilai maksimal Rp 5 triliun", which at 5,125 is ~0.79% of the 122.8bn shares; assumptions.share_change retires 0.5% in FY2026 and nothing after, and the basis gives no reason for the 0.5% (it says "roughly 0.8% of shares; assume 0.5% retired"). The report also never credits the third 2026 interim dividend that S8 says is planned ("dividen interim sebanyak tiga kali pada 2026"), which is a cash-timing benefit to the DDM that the model's mid-year convention does not capture.
challenges.answer: The buyback is now modelled at the authorised 0.8% of shares rather than 0.5%, and the basis gives the reason: at today's price the Rp5tn authorisation is 0.79% of the register and BCA has executed the programmes it authorises. The third interim is addressed rather than ignored: S8 states the board may pay three interims in 2026 and that every interim is deducted from the final dividend, so it is a timing benefit and not a payout increase; the report says the mid-year convention in the dividend model understates the cash slightly and that the payout is unaffected, which is more accurate than carrying an extra dividend that would double count.

challenges.challenge: "It is the lowest of the three because the payout of 72% leaves a fifth of earnings outside the model" is wrong on its own table: DDM is Rp6,225, residual income Rp6,615 and justified P/BV Rp4,926 — the DDM is the middle method, Rp1,299 above the primary. The sentence is the only explanation the report gives for the method dispersion, and it points the reader at the wrong number while the primary method (the one that says the shares are 3.9% expensive) is left unexplained.
challenges.answer: The sentence is corrected and the ordering is now stated explicitly: the multiple is the lowest at {{val.methods.justified_pbv.value|px}}, the dividend stream is {{val.methods.ddm.vs_primary_pct|pctv}} above it and residual income {{val.methods.residual_income.vs_primary_pct|pctv}} above it, so the dividend model is the middle method and the earlier "lowest of the three" was wrong on the report's own table. The dispersion is explained rather than asserted: the multiple is a single-period capitalisation of the spread between the sustainable return and the cost of equity on a book value struck today, while the other two discount a stream over ten explicit years, so the multiple cannot see the book compounding and the dividend model cannot see the capital left behind — residual income sees both, which is why it is the highest. That is also the direct answer to why the half-weighted method is the outlier and not the anchor: it is the one that discards the compounding, so the report does not treat its 3.9% shortfall as the central case, and it says in the valuation section that the reverse solve — which runs on this method — is the place the reader should test that judgement.

missing_bull_case.note: Two sourced upsides are absent or neutralised. (1) The multiple: the model's own own_history shows a four-year mean P/BV of 4.41x (FY2022A 4.77, FY2023A 4.78, FY2024A 4.54, FY2025A 3.53) against 2.24x on the FY2025A book and 2.07x forward — the stock has de-rated ~50% and sits 41% below the pack's 52-week high of 8,700. The report never puts the current multiple against that history and instead asserts it is roughly where BCA traded in benign times, which understates the largest available upside (a return to even 3.0x book on the same BVPS of 2,288 is Rp6,864, above the target). (2) The GWM cut is the only sourced positive catalyst (S12: 2pp cut, BCA gets liquidity relief "mendekati 1 persen") and the assumptions consume it as an offset to deposit competition that is never quantified.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear case omits the channel the report itself names. §2 says the balance-of-payments regime reaches this name through the sovereign yield and the cost of equity, and §5's bear narrative repeats that "the sovereign yield stays high" — but the bear shocks only credit_cost, nim and loan_growth, so no discount-rate shock is applied. valuation_method_fit.note: The BANKS card makes residual income the engine and warranted P/BV the cross-check; the draft gives P/BV 50% and RI 30%, and calls that "weighted as the industry card prescribes" — the card prescribes no weights. That inversion matters because the 50%-weighted method (4,926) is the one 3.9% BELOW the price and it is what drags the blend to 5,693. Worse, the reverse solve is run on justified_pbv (fund record reverse_dcf method justified_pbv, FY2027E, implied 0.4878%) but its conclusion is stated against the blended target. And the method card's required output — deposit beta and the CASA/TD mix path against the BI path, with the deck's bi_rate 5.75% FY2027E — is absent entirely: NIM is held flat with no deposit-beta or mix argument, and no macro variable enters the model, only the prose.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose claims more than the numbers show in three places. §5 says "a bank trading at a premium to book loses more from a margin shock than it gains from an equal and opposite improvement" — the model says the opposite: bear 4,619 is -1,410 from base while bull 7,810 is +1,781, which is why the weighted target (6,122) sits 1.5% above the base (6,029). §4 says the DDM "is the lowest of the three" when P/BV at 4,926 is Rp1,299 lower. conservatism_audit.note: Named, each without a source or against one: (1) NIM held at the 9M average of 5.41% while Q3 alone is 5.6% and rising 5.32 -> 5.41 -> 5.6 (F23, S10) — the base does not carry the reported acceleration, worth ~0.2pp TA-equivalent, ~2.5% of NP; (2) the GWM liquidity benefit (~1% of deposits, ~Rp13tn) is assumed offset by unnamed deposit competition; (3) credit cost 0.8% held for ten years against a reverse-implied 0.49% and comps BMRI 0.65%; (4) buyback modelled at 0.5% of shares against 0.8% authorised for no stated reason; (5) terminal growth 4.0% against nominal GDP of ~8.6% in the same deck and internal capital generation of ROE x retention = 6.2% — the bank is assumed to shrink its balance sheet growth to 4% while retaining enough capital for 6.2%. findings.finding: The base case is sound but its near-term phasing is not drawn. FY2026E net profit is Rp63,266.7bn, +10.0% on FY2025A, while 9M-2026 net profit is Rp45,200bn, +4.2% (S2, F37), and H1-2026 was Rp29,500bn (same S2 page), so Q3-2026 alone was Rp15,700bn. Reaching FY2026E therefore requires a Q4 of about Rp18,070bn: +15% on Q3 and +28% on Q4-2025 (Rp14,157bn). No driver in the model produces that step - NIM, CTI and credit cost are flat - and section 3 does not reconcile the full-year forecast to the nine-month actual. Section 3 does disclose that the modelled margin sits above both Q3 prints, which is the honest half of the point, but the profit bridge is missing.

The front-matter summary and thesis bullet 1 still juxtapose the 9M-2026 CASA of Rp1,103,000bn with a 79.5% loan-to-deposit ratio, which is the FY2025 ratio (993,000/1,249,000); the 9M ratio is 81.7%.
